Stiff-Man Syndrome — Diagnostic Criteria and Pitfalls
T Kuruvilla*, NE Bharucha**, EJ Thompson***, M Hawa****, V Chauhan**, R Agarwal**
The stiff-man syndrome is a very rare neurological dis-
ease characterized by progressive and fluctuating muscle
rigidity, with initial involvement of the abdominal and lum-
bar paraspinal muscles:! The rarity of the condition can
cause confusion in diagnosis especially in the early stages.
We describe a man who presented with features of the syn-
drome but who was initially thought to have peritonitis.
A 40 years old man with normal family and personal his-
tory developed a low grade fever associated with a feeling
of tightness of the anteridg abdominal muscles. The fever
subsided after a few days but the stiffness of the muscles
persisted and over the following days also involved the
thoracolumbar paraspinal muscles. The stiffness was con-
tinuous but exertion and stress would cause painful spasms
of the same muscle groups. Routine blood and urine tests
and imaging studies of the abdomen were normal. The per-
sistent rigidity of the abdominal muscles with a prior
history of fever raised the possibility of an underlying peri-
tonitis. Hospitalization and parenteral antibiotics did not
relieve the symptoms. The possibility of tetanus was also
considered but thought unlikely in view of the atypical pro-
gression of illness.
Symptoms gradually progressed over the next few weeks
and the patient was referred to our hospital for further in-
vestigations. On examination, there was marked hypertonia
in the anterior abdominal and thoracolumbar paraspinal
muscles with an exaggerated lumbar lordosis with scoliosis
which persisted at rest. Forward flexion was markedly re-
stricted. Neurological examination was otherwise normal.
Vital parameters and the other systems were also normal.
Electromyography studies did not show any changes of a
primary muscle disease but there were spontaneous normal
motor unit potentials over the abdominal and paraspinal
muscles even at rest which decreased after intravenous ad-
ministration of diazepam. The silent period and nerve
conduction studies were normal. Blood investigations, espe-
cially blood sugar and serum electrolytes were also within
normal limits. Serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) were

sent to London for autoantibody studies. Glutamic acid de-
carboxylase (GAD) antibodies were strongly positive in
both serum and CSF and islet cell antibodies were present
in serum at high titres (> 80 Juvenile Diabetes Foundation
Units - normal < 10). The patient was started on diazepam
and baclofen, the doses of which were progressively in-
creased to 30 and 60 mg per day respectively. With this,
there was a significant decrease in the muscle rigidity and
spasm, the lumbar lordosis decreased and the scoliosis dis-
appeared.
The above patient had most of the classical features of
the stiff-man syndrome: onset in middle age; stiffness in-
itially involving the trunk muscles with persistence of
rigidity even at rest; superimposed painful spasms precipi-
tated by stress and exertion; hyperlordosis of lumbar spine

with restricted forward flexion; gradual progression over
months; otherwise normal neurological examination with
normal higher functions, motor power, sensations and re-
flexes; characteristic EMG changes of continuous normal
motor unit activity at rest in affected muscles with no signs
of denervation or primary muscle disease and normal nerve
conduction studies. The presence of GAD and islet - cell
antibodies in our patient supports the hypothesis of an
autoimmune basis for the pathogenesis of the syndrome.”
Many affected patients develop diabetes mellitus and other
autoimmune disorders but these were not found in our pa-
tient.
Extrapyramidal syndromes like torsion dystonias, pro-
gressive encephalomyelitis, spinal cord lesions, localized
tetanus, Issac’s syndrome and myotonia can closely mimic
the stiff - man syndrome.'* These and other local patholo-
gies like peritonitis can be differentiated by the classical
features of the disease together with electrophysiological
studies but a high index of suspicion is also required in the
early stages.
